Photograph: PA/Alamy View image in fullscreen Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London, where Aalim Ahmed died after falling from the 15th floor in May 2024. Photograph: PA/Alamy Housing London flat where boy fell to death could have had more safeguards, inquest told Aalim Ahmed, five, fell from 15th-floor window at tower block family had asked to be moved out of, court hears Nadeem Badshah Wed 19 Aug 2026 14.51 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 18.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An inquest into the death of a five-year-old boy who fell from a 15th-floor window has heard that more measures could have been taken to make it safer. Aalim Ahmed, who was autistic, died when he fell from a kitchen window at a residential block in Plaistow, east London. His father, Makail Ahmed, rushed from the top floor temporary social housing flat and discovered his body shortly before 6am on 16 May 2024. There was a long history of complaints about the council accommodation from the family, who had asked to be moved, the court heard. East London coroner’s court heard that the Newham council property manager Nnenna Muoma thought “more restricted features could have been installed” after visiting the Ahmed family on the afternoon he died. In a note to the council after seeing the family at Jacobs House, the property manager wrote: “Following the horrible incident and fatality, I visited the family yesterday. The kitchen window from where the child fell off is functional but can be operated by a child, hence the incident. “There is [a] restricted feature to allow a limited opening. More restricted features could have been installed to reduce this risk.” Muoma told the court: “That was my personal thought. I have seen other households with children with special needs with different gadgets which can be done to make it safer.” She said she was not an expert in the area and did not know the window restrictors in place could be locked. View image in fullscreen The family had asked to be moved from Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News. Makail Ahmed and Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, have described their son’s death as “preventable” and blamed Newham council, after claims safety concerns about the flat were reported on multiple occasions. A postmortem examination found Aalim died from “multiple injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height”. Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, because her son had “no sense of danger”. She felt the property was not suitable for her young family, which also included a newborn girl, but felt obliged to take it or risk homelessness. On the day Aalim died, Osman was sitting on a bed with her arms wrapped around herself when Muoma saw her. One of the first things Osman told her was: “I asked to be moved and nobody listened to me.” Muoma told the court: “I said I do not have that information but I am sorry. We want to assist you and if [you] cannot stay overnight I can find you a place to stay.” Muoma said she tried the window twice and was able to open it on the second attempt, but could not remember exactly how she did it. The council property manager said she may have pressed a button to help open it but did not give details about the restrictor or the position of the handle. She also took a photograph of the open position to show her manager how far it could open, she told the court. Newham council said it would be unable to comment until after the inquest concluded. The hearing continues. https://monocle.com/culture/books-to-rea.text: Subscribe | British Pound (GBP) Euro (EUR) US Dollar (USD) Australian Dollar (AUD) Swiss Franc (CHF) At its best, a summer reading list isn’t one list at all. It’s a set of options matched to conditions and mood. What you might want to read on a plane isn’t the same as what you’d want to read on a beach lounger at 16.00, half asleep and sun-drunk – or even drunk-drunk. It’s about finding books that match both mindset and situation. Long-haul flights need scale, something big enough to swallow the hours. Poolside afternoons need pace and perhaps a little mischief, narratives you can dip in and out of without losing the thread. A warm evening on a terrace is for a story that could spark your dinner conversation. And when the rain comes, reach for something a little more weighty. As the host of Meet the Writers on Monocle Radio , I’ve read many different books in many different places. I’ve learned the key to choosing a good book is to match it to the place you’re in and the weather in your head, not just the conditions outside. Here are 14 titles that do just that. 1. ‘The Odyssey’ Homer, translated by Emily Wilson Ancient Greece Good for: Long-haul flights or beside a wine-dark sea. Homer invented travel writing. The Odyssey tells the story of a man trying to get home and everything standing in his way. Emily Wilson’s translation – the first complete English translation of the book by a woman – presents a modern take on the ancient work with far more attention paid to the women, the enslaved people and the power structures that were brushed over by earlier translators. Read the book and you can weave it into discussions about the Christopher Nolan film that was released in cinemas this summer. 2. ‘Jan Morris: A Life’ Sara Wheeler United Kingdom Good for: Waiting at a departure lounge. Jan Morris was a prolific Welsh journalist and writer, whose work encompassed travel writing, foreign correspondence and everything in between. Sara Wheeler’s biography does justice to a genuinely singular life, including Morris’s transition, and the decades spent writing about Europe’s cities with real love and precision and questions of identity. Few people saw more of the world or wrote about it with less vanity. 3. ‘Lázár’ Nelio Biedermann Switzerland and Hungary Good for: A week away, when you want a century in your carry bag. Lázár follows a Hungarian family across a century of upheaval, from the Habsburg Empire to the First World War, through fascism, Soviet occupation and the 1956 uprising. Impressively, Nelio Biedermann was only 22 years old when the book was published earlier this year. This is a big, confident book from someone barely out of his teens and one of this year’s genuine European discoveries. 4. ‘Baldwin: A Love Story’ Nicholas Boggs Brooklyn, Leukerbad, the south of France and Istanbul Good for: Relaxed mornings, coffee on the boulevard. Washington-born Nicholas Boggs tells James Baldwin’s life story through the people who loved him and the people he loved, from mentor Beauford Delaney to Lucien Happersberger, the Swiss painter who became his first great love in Paris. The story goes from Brooklyn and the south of France to Paris, Tuscany and Istanbul, and the months at Happersberger’s family chalet in Leukerbad, Switzerland, that gave Baldwin the isolation to finish his debut novel, Go Tell It on the Mountain . Listen to a conversation with Boggs on ‘Meet the Writers ’. 5. ‘The Disappearers’ Marlon James Jamaica and the US Good for: Intellectual stimulation on the second week of holiday. Marlon James won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings and he’s back on this year’s long list for The Disappearers . The latter book takes place in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988: eight gay men gather to rehearse a play. Though they are strangers to each other, they’re bound by the one thing they can’t mention. One night a mob violently attacks the group and what follows is a story about the aftermath. This is not a gentle book. 6. ‘The Shadow of the Object’ Chloe Aridjis Mexico, the Netherlands and USA Good for: An overcast afternoon indoors when you want something a little uncanny. Chloe Aridjis grew up shuttling between Mexico, the Netherlands and the US, and that unsettled quality runs through her fiction: it’s visual, faintly eerie and never quite goes where you expect it to. The Shadow of the Object opens with a dog bite from the elderly family German Shepherd and moves through a Mexico City hospital ward, an unlikely friendship and magic lanterns. The book made this year’s Booker longlist. Listen to a conversation with Aridjis on ‘Meet the Writers’. 7. ‘Netherwood’ Jake Arnott UK Good for: Late-night reading, when you’re feeling brave. A literary thriller built around Aleister Crowley and Britain’s occult undercurrent, including the communes, the counterculture and the folk horror lurking behind the picturesque seaside postcards. Jake Arnott has always been drawn to Britain’s alternative histories, and Netherwood is him at his most atmospheric, mixing fact and fiction. You might not want to read it alone, though: it’s pretty scary. 8. ‘Our Last Resort’ Clémence Michallon France Good for: A languid afternoon on a yacht or at a resort. A French writer’s take on an American obsession, a luxury resort in Utah, a group of cult survivors trying to rebuild and a murder. Michallon brings an outsider’s eye to a very American kind of story, which is part of what makes it work. A fast-pace read for the poolside. 9. ‘Lust’ Erika Lust Sweden and Spain Good for: Sharp, sexy thinking. The aptly named Erika Lust grew up in a Swedish household that didn’t talk about sex, then moved to Barcelona and built one of the best-known adult film studios. The book argues that porn is a mirror of society’s problems rather than the cause. Part memoir, part feminist rallying cry, Lust goes behind the scenes on the film sets, into the casting and the consent conversations, and makes the case for pleasure as something worth taking seriously. Intelligent rather than sensational. 10. ‘All Fours’ Miranda July USA Good for: Reading with a book club. Sexually frank and very funny, Miranda July’s novel takes on midlife desire, a marriage under pressure, menopause and reinvention. Pair it with Lust for the same subject from two directions: one fiction, one criticism. You will have an opinion and so will everyone else who reads it. 11. ‘Exit Wounds’ Peter Godwin Zimbabwe, UK and US Good for: A family holiday or the flight home. This one is personal: Peter Godwin is my brother. Exit Wounds moves between Zimbabwe, London, New York and Lakeville. It’s about family, war, exile, ageing parents, a marriage ending and three strong women. We’re touring Western Australia together with the book in October. If you’re there, come and have a chat. Or just buy it and I’ll get a drink out of my share of the royalties. Cheers. Listen to an interview with Godwin on ‘Meet the Writers’. 12. ‘Attention-Seeking Behaviour’ Aea Varfis-van Warmelo UK and Greece Good for: A train journey, or when you need something to argue about. The narrator is a compulsive liar and she tells you upfront. A young London journalist, she spins outlandish stories, trying to work out where the lying started and what it has cost her. Woven through the book is a real history of lie detection, from Ekman’s discredited theory that a flash of expression gives away what someone truly feels to the polygraph’s long and shaky career in policing. Fiction, memoir and essay run together, I found it utterly compelling. 13. ‘Astronaut!’ Oana Aristide Romania, Greece and Sweden Good for: A rainy day when you want something darkly funny. Romania, 1989, the final months of Nicolae Ceaușescu’s rule. A detective is told to pin a string of murders on a man-eating bear rather than admit a serial killer is loose in a country where killers officially don’t exist. Meanwhile, an eight-year-old girl gets pulled into her elderly neighbour’s plot against the regime. It is dark and funny and examines what it costs to keep believing an obvious lie. Aristide is a co-founder of the Syros Literary Festival (with me and my brother), which we’ll be holding in the Hotel Aristide Hotel in Greece in April. Come along to meet Oana and many others on this list. Listen to a conversation with Aristide on ‘Meet the Writers’. 14. ‘Porcupines’ Fran Fabriczki Hungary and USA Good for: Reading at an airport bar. Szonja arrives in Los Angeles from Budapest at 18 for what’s meant to be a summer visit and never quite leaves. The book moves between Cold War Washington, late-Communist Budapest and the bright sunshine of early 2000s Los Angeles. The title comes from Arthur Schopenhauer’s fable about porcupines huddling together for warmth and pricking each other in the process. https://www.politico.eu/article/ia-des-d.text: BRUXELLES — Les députés européens font pression pour élargir le champ d'application de la réglementation phare de l'UE en matière d'IA afin de tenir les géants américains de la tech pour responsables des risques que leurs modèles les plus avancés font peser sur l'humanité, selon des échanges écrits consultés par POLITICO. La proposition émanant de quatre élus de premier plan du Parlement européen viserait à ajouter de nouvelles règles à l' AI Act , le règlement européen sur l'intelligence artificielle de 2024, afin de garantir que des entreprises telles qu'OpenAI et Anthropic puissent être tenues pour responsables lorsque leur technologie est utilisée de manière imprévue. Cette initiative montre que Bruxelles prend conscience d'une réalité dans laquelle les dommages causés par l'IA sont déjà une réalité et où les risques se multiplient — et elle marque la première tentative concrète au sein de l'UE visant à répondre aux craintes concernant la sécurité de l'IA, qui dominent actuellement l'agenda politique mondial. Advertisement Advertisement Le groupe appelle la Commission à présenter une loi sur la responsabilité en matière d’IA “afin de combler les lacunes législatives qui existent actuellement concernant ce type d’incidents, de sorte qu’aucun citoyen ni aucune entreprise européenne ne se retrouve sans recours face à ces grands prestataires lorsqu’ils causent un préjudice”, selon une note adressée à l’exécutif européen le 16 septembre et consultée par POLITICO. Pour l'eurodéputée néerlandaise Kim van Sparrentak, membre des Verts et du groupe d'élus chargés de suivre la mise en œuvre des règles de l'UE en matière d'IA au Parlement, l'évolution rapide de cette technologie oblige l'UE à actualiser sans délai ce qui était, il y a deux ans, la première législation contraignante d'envergure au monde visant à réglementer les modèles avancés d'intelligence artificielle. “L'Europe doit reprendre les devants”, a plaidé Kim van Sparrentak, qui fait partie des quatre eurodéputés à la tête de cette initiative aux côtés du conservateur allemand Axel Voss, du social-démocrate italien Brando Benifei et de l'indépendant irlandais Michael McNamara. Cet appel a reçu le soutien de députés du Parti populaire européen (centre droit), des groupes des Socialistes et démocrates et des libéraux de Renew, ce qui témoigne d'un large soutien politique. Une menace existentielle pour l’humanité Cette semaine marque une nouvelle étape importante pour les efforts mondiaux en matière de sécurité de l’intelligence artificielle, après un été marqué par de nombreux incidents de piratage liés à l’IA et des avertissements sur la menace existentielle qu’elle représenterait pour l’humanité. Ce sujet est au cœur des débats de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies à New York et d’une réunion ce mardi des ministres du Numérique du G7, et il occupera le sommet qui se tiendra cette semaine entre le dirigeant chinois Xi Jinping et le président américain Donald Trump. L'appel lancé par les députés européens met en lumière les lacunes de l' AI Act , qui avait été adoptée à une époque où l'idée que des agents d'IA puissent pirater d'autres entreprises relevait davantage de la science-fiction. Advertisement Advertisement Les règles relatives à la responsabilité en matière d'IA pourraient permettre aux victimes de préjudices causés par cette technologie d'obtenir plus facilement et à moindre coût une indemnisation, par exemple en faisant peser la charge de la preuve sur les entreprises. Cet intérêt nouveau pour la responsabilité du fait des produits en Europe serait également en phase avec certaines positions exprimées aux Etats-Unis, notamment le soutien apporté par l’ancien Monsieur IA de Donald Trump, David Sacks, lors du POLITICO Decoded Summit, qui s'est tenu à Washington la semaine dernière. La proposition des députés européens d'introduire de nouvelles règles en matière de responsabilité marque un revirement radical par rapport à la position officielle adoptée par l'UE ces derniers mois. Pendant des semaines, Bruxelles a apporté une réponse toute faite à la série d’incidents liés à l’IA, aux avertissements des chercheurs et aux appels de dirigeants de la tech à ralentir son développement : l' AI Act est déjà là pour empêcher les entreprises de perdre le contrôle de leurs modèles ou de leurs agents. Cette nouvelle attention portée à la responsabilité constitue un aveu tacite que la législation sur l'IA ne suffira pas à elle seule. Mais cet appel à instaurer de nouvelles règles pose également des difficultés sur le plan législatif. L'UE vient en effet de réviser l'ensemble de son dispositif régissant la conformité des produits aux normes de sécurité, dans le cadre d'une mise à jour de ses règles générales en matière de responsabilité du fait des produits, qui doit entrer en vigueur le 9 décembre. Advertisement Advertisement Bruxelles ambitionne également d'alléger davantage la réglementation dans le domaine des technologies, dans le but de “simplifier” les règles afin de favoriser la croissance des entreprises. Des règles spécifiques en matière de responsabilité liées à l'IA avaient été proposées par la Commission européenne en septembre 2022, mais celle-ci les a retirées l'année dernière. Protections juridiques La réglementation actuelle de l'UE intègre déjà une approche de l'IA sous l'angle de la sécurité des produits. Elle incite les entreprises à évaluer leurs modèles ou applications d'IA et à déterminer le risque qu'ils présentent pour le public : inacceptable, élevé, limité ou minime. Mais la loi ne fait pas grand-chose pour remédier aux dommages causés. La loi ne s'applique pas non plus aux modèles d'IA avant leur déploiement, pendant leur phase d'entraînement ou de test, même si la plupart des piratages de l'été dernier ont été menés par des agents alimentés par des modèles de recherche à usage exclusivement interne. “Le fonctionnement actuel du système ne reconnaît pratiquement aucun droit aux personnes lésées par l’intelligence artificielle”, a pointé Mario Mariniello, chercheur senior spécialisé dans les questions numériques et de concurrence au sein du think tank Bruegel. “Cela réduit les incitations pour les développeurs à prendre en compte ce risque et, par conséquent, d’investir dans la sécurité.” Pour les experts en cybersécurité, les incidents survenus cet été, à l'image du piratage de Hugging Face par des agents développés par OpenAI, sont la preuve qu'il est nécessaire d'avoir un régime de responsabilité. Advertisement Advertisement “Je ne pense pas qu’il soit judicieux d’affirmer que, sous prétexte qu’il n’y avait pas d’intention criminelle et que c’est un agent d’IA qui a agi, il n’y a pas de responsabilité juridique”, a estimé Marcus Hutchins, un expert britannique en cybersécurité surtout connu pour avoir mis fin à une attaque mondiale du rançongiciel WannaCry en 2017. Certains experts, comme Irene Kamara, maître de conférences à l’université de Tilburg, ont souligné le fait que les agents d’IA sont souvent anthropomorphisés, comme s’il s’agissait de protagonistes à l’apparence humaine lançant une attaque de leur propre chef : cela “détourne l’attention de la recherche du ou des véritables responsables de l’incident”, a-t-elle soulevé. Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.
